name: Red Flags in Tech Claims
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Tells: Common Red Flags Across Every Hyped Technology
lesson.summary: Beyond a checklist of questions to ask, there is a recognizable set of patterns that show up again and again across hyped technology claims of every kind, and learning to spot them is a general-purpose skill.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter gave you questions to ask. This chapter gives you patterns to recognize on sight, the kind of thing that, once you have seen it a few times, starts jumping out at you in every press release and product launch you encounter.

Vague superlatives standing in for numbers are one of the most common tells. Words like "revolutionary," "unprecedented," or "breakthrough" carry no measurable content on their own. A specific, verifiable number, this many percent faster, this many fewer errors, this specific baseline being beaten, is worth more than a page of superlatives, and a claim that leans entirely on adjectives instead of numbers is worth extra scrutiny.

Demonstrations that cannot be independently reproduced are another. If a result was shown under conditions fully controlled by the organization making the claim, using data or methods they will not disclose, outside experts have no way to check the work, and "trust us" is doing a great deal of load-bearing work in the story.

Weak baseline comparisons are a subtler version of the same problem. A new result compared against an old, unoptimized, or deliberately hobbled alternative will always look more impressive than one compared against the actual best available option. This is one of the more common tricks in technology benchmarking generally, not unique to quantum computing.

Recall the concept of redefining success covered earlier in this course. Watch for cases where an organization's original promise was ambitious and specific, and years later, after that promise did not pan out on schedule, success gets quietly redefined into something narrower and easier to claim, announced with exactly the same triumphant tone as if the original goal had been met. The tell is not that the goal changed, goals legitimately change as understanding improves. The tell is when nobody acknowledges that it changed.

Timing is worth watching too. Major claims that cluster suspiciously close to funding rounds, public offerings, or budget votes deserve a second look, not because timing alone proves anything, but because it identifies exactly the moments when the incentive to overstate is strongest.

And finally, watch for claims that stay conspicuously silent about the costs, overhead, error rates, or practical caveats that this entire course has spent so much time on for quantum computing specifically. A technology story that only ever tells you the upside, and never mentions the tradeoffs a genuinely rigorous account would include, is telling you something by what it leaves out.

No single one of these red flags proves a claim is false. Real breakthroughs happen, and sometimes they really do look this impressive. But when several of these patterns stack up in the same announcement, that stack is information, and it earns the claim more scrutiny before you pass it along as settled fact.
